abstract: Pregnancy requires coordinated maternal adaptations to support fetal growth, yet signals that couple gestation to intestinal remodeling remain poorly defined. Here, we show that pregnancy induces a reversible regenerative program in the small intestine characterized by villus elongation, increased nutrient transporter expression, and enhanced absorptive capacity driven by intestinal stem cell (ISC) hyperproliferation. Using single-cell transcriptomic and genetic approaches, we identify intestinal regulatory T (Treg) cells as required regulators of this remodeling. Estradiol treatment of ovariectomized mice fully recapitulated the gestational intestinal remodeling phenotype, whereas Treg-specific deletion of estrogen receptor  reduced villus expansion and impaired nutrient absorption. Mechanistically, elevated estradiol levels during pregnancy expand Treg cells and enhance IL-10 production, which directly promotes ISC proliferation and epithelial renewal. Cross-species analyses in mice and pigs support conservation of the intestinal phenotype, while integration of human GWAS data links Treg-associated IL-10 signaling to birth-weight-associated traits. Together, these findings demonstrate that pregnancy repurposes immune tolerance pathways to coordinate maternal intestinal remodeling with fetal nutritional demands.

summary: Pregnancy-driven estradiol signaling expands intestinal Treg cells that secrete IL-10 to promote stem cell proliferation and small intestine remodeling in mice.
